items.content:
In the near term (definitely not in the long term), more capable models should mean safer models (maybe paradoxically).

Current models are unsafe not because they're too smart, but because they take goals too literally or take nonsensical shortcuts to achieve these goals, i.e. they're RL-fried. They lack common sense. They don't do the right thing in the face of ambiguity. Basically, they're not smart enough. They're at that dangerous level where they're smart enough to achieve goals but not smart enough to tell if they're pursuing the right goals or achieving them in a sensible way.

More capable models can be safely trusted with more complex goals -- I personally feel like Astra is much safer for my codebase than Sol.

This is often framed as an alignment problem, but really it's an intelligence problem.

I cannot emphasize enough how much GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 are already enough for transformative impact in large sections of the economy. They can reliably do weeks worth of human work when properly guided & harnessed.

Those effects will not be all at once and be uneven, but the fact that change will occur is inevitable no matter how the frontier is paced. But inevitable change does not mean the type of change is inevitable. It is increasingly important that we develop & share models of AI-human work that enhance, rather than only replace, human labor. The labs have a role to play in doing this, but so do companies and industries experimenting with AI adoption, as well as policy makers who can incentivize this sort of inplemenation.

This work is important regardless of existential risk, and needs a lot more focus.

items.content:
The entire conversation about the dangers of building superintelligence (not a hypothetical one, but the one that will soon emerge from LLM scaling) is so ridiculous to me that I really wish I didn't know that this conversation is happening and people with some reputation in tech and science are seriously participating in it.

There's not a single indication that LLMs can be significantly improved beyond cases with verifiable rewards, which currently include only two: math derivations and coding.

Maybe math and coding are what *you* do most of the time at work, but it's not even one percent of what *people* do for a living!

How can so many educated people be so narrow-minded?! It blows my mind.

items.content:
Introducing FlyOCR 🪰 - I trained a fly brain to read a PDF

It uses the full MaleCNS v1.0 fruit fly connectcome. The architecture is inspired by doomfly by @nftechie_

The fly splits a pdf image into individual glyphs, maps pixels into receptor activations, runs simplified current-based dynamics across the 166k neurons and 25m edges in the circuit, applies a compact readout model on the downstream spikes, and concatenates everything into the parsed output.

On reading an actual Microsoft 10-k, the fly gets ~86% over the balance sheet heading, but is largely able to read the numeric values correctly. Over 1.7k+ sampled glyphs (chars+digits) it gets 87% accuracy. With enough training it might match some of the latter-generation MNIST models!

Maybe eventually we’ll replace our doc parsing VLMs with flies.

Full video below.

items.title: Neural networks must often transform entangled data representations into linearly separable ones for...
items.content:
Neural networks must often transform entangled data representations into linearly separable ones for accurate classification. When class manifolds are linked in low-dimensional space, this requires changing topological invariants such as the linking number, which counts how many times one closed curve or manifold winds through another. This work examines this constraint by restricting network width to three dimensions throughout, allowing direct tracking of linking numbers layer by layer while isolating the effects of depth, activation choice, and architectural features.

The in this paper analysis proves that width-three feedforward networks using monotonic activations such as ReLU, sigmoid, or tanh preserve linking numbers exactly. Invertible affine layers act as homeomorphisms that maintain the invariant up to sign, and monotonic activations permit straight-line homotopies that keep the images of linked components disjoint. Consequently, no depth of such a network can unlink data whose linking number is nonzero, imposing an accuracy ceiling on classification tasks. In contrast, ResNets synthesize nonmonotonic folding operations through skip connections, pure transformers approximate the same folds via attention, and nonmonotonic activations such as GELU or Swish perform folding directly. All three mechanisms break the homotopy argument and enable unlinking at the same narrow width.

"Game theory: An open access textbook with 165 solved exercises" by Giacomo Bonanno (2015) is now in @ChapterPal's collection.

This textbook offers an introduction to non-cooperative game theory designed for advanced undergraduate and graduate students, instructors, and researchers in economics, political science, computer science, logic, and philosophy.

The book investigates non-cooperative game theory, modeling interactive situations where independent, rational individuals pursue well-defined objectives without the ability to sign binding contracts or form binding coalitions.

The material follows a structured progression, advancing systematically from basic decision frames to advanced epistemic and extensive-form models.

The opening chapters establish foundational tools using ordinal payoffs, where player preferences are represented purely through qualitative rankings. Within this setting, the text examines strategic-form games, strict and weak dominance, iterated deletion procedures, pure-strategy Nash equilibrium, and extensive-form game trees with perfect and imperfect information solved via backward induction and subgame perfection.

The book then broadens its scope to cardinal payoffs, covering von Neumann-Morgenstern expected utility theory, risk attitudes, compound lotteries, mixed strategies, and behavioral strategies in dynamic games.

items.content:
The Advanced Calculus (2nd edition) textbook by Gerald B. Folland (2023) is now in @ChapterPal's collection.

The textbook provides a rigorous, analysis-based treatment of multivariable calculus and classical analysis for advanced undergraduate students in mathematics, physical sciences, and engineering. It assumes that readers are already familiar with basic single-variable calculus, standard computational techniques, and elementary linear algebra. The text bridges introductory calculus and higher-level mathematical analysis by establishing a firm theoretical groundwork while maintaining a strong connection to geometric intuition and physical applications.

The material opens with the topology and geometry of Euclidean spaces, introducing limits, continuity, completeness, compactness, and connectedness. From these foundations, the text develops multivariable differential calculus, using linear approximations and the Fréchet derivative as the unifying framework for directional derivatives, the chain rule, Taylor expansions, and extrema classification. A central focus is the local solvability of nonlinear systems through the implicit and inverse mapping theorems, which are applied to analyze coordinate transformations, functional dependence, and the representation of smooth curves and higher-dimensional surfaces embedded in Euclidean space.

items.content:
Every single true crime documentary on Netflix screams: Don't talk to the police! Don't talk to the police! Don't talk to the police!

In virtually every documentary out there, you see how the system is failing victims and witnesses, betraying and destroying good people.

The fact that some people, like Caroline in this docuseries, still do the right thing despite mental struggles and blatant disregard of her situation by the law enforcement and victim protection services, is heartbreaking to watch.

She decided to betray a person she truly loved, gave the prosecution everything they needed, and they wiped their feet on her, blamed her for not being an exemplary witness, and moved on.

Any smart person will not go to the police in a similar situation after watching this documentary, or any other.

I always tell my kids: "Don't say anything to the police other than 'No comment' and 'I need my lawyer.' By doing what you think is the right thing, you dig yourself a grave."
